27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	[A] To benchmark open-weight against frontier LLMs on function-level vulnerability detection, treating monetary cost and energy as "first-class axes alongside detection quality" (p. 1). The study also calibrates the LLM results against non-LLM reference points (static analysers and learned detectors) "to gauge absolute difficulty" (p. 2). [A] The authors claim the conjunction is new (a security task, a five-model open roster, and cost and energy as per-task axes), "not ... a priority" on any single axis (p. 3).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- [V] No numbered RQs. Contributions are framed as (p. 2):
33	  - a cost- and energy-aware open-vs-frontier benchmark on label-clean PrimeVul with non-LLM reference points;
34	  - evidence on the quality–efficiency Pareto frontier;
35	  - an account of what can and cannot be measured for closed API models.
36	- [I] Implicit questions:
37	  1. Are open-weight LLMs competitive with frontier LLMs in quality?
38	  2. Are they more cost- and energy-efficient?
39	  3. How do LLMs compare with SAST and fine-tuned detectors at realistic prevalence?
40	
41	## 3. Methodology
42	- Research design: [V] Empirical benchmark of binary function-level detection ("does this C/C++ function contain a vulnerability?") on a fixed stratified PrimeVul sample (p. 4). Additional analyses (pp. 9–20):
43	  - re-scoring at the natural 1:44 prevalence;
44	  - configuration-matched families A/B/C;
45	  - prompt, sample-draw and run-to-run robustness;
46	  - a reasoning-vs-direct replication across two measurement epochs.
47	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Eight LLMs prompted zero-shot through a unified OpenAI-compatible API gateway (p. 4, Table 2). [V] The gateway is **not named** (pp. 4, 29).
48	  - **Frontier:** Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`); active parameters assumed ~100B for the energy estimate.
49	  - **Open-weight:** DeepSeek-V3.2 (~37B active), GLM-5 (~32B active), Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-Coder-30B (3B active MoE), Gemma-3-4B.
50	  - [V] Pinned providers and precision: DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 at GMICloud FP8; Llama-3.3-70B at DeepInfra FP8; Qwen3-Coder-30B at SiliconFlow FP8; Gemma-3-4B at DeepInfra bf16 (p. 29, Table A2).
51	  - [V] Main configuration: direct answer, reasoning disabled where permitted. Gemini cannot disable reasoning (HTTP 400) (p. 4, p. 29).
52	  - [V] Prompt: a security-reviewer persona; answer YES/NO first, then an optional explanation (p. 28). A lenient parser counts unparseable outputs as parse failures, not "safe" (p. 4, p. 29).
53	- Baselines or comparison conditions:
54	  - [V] **Trivial baselines:** always-safe and always-vulnerable (p. 7, Table 4); always-flag at 1:44 prevalence (p. 8, Table 5).
55	  - [V] **SAST arm** (p. 6, p. 10, Table 7): Flawfinder 2.0.20 (lexical), Cppcheck 2.21 (flow-sensitive), Semgrep 1.175 with community C and security-audit rulesets (pattern plus intraprocedural taint). A function is flagged if any finding reaches a swept severity threshold.
56	  - [V] **DL arm:**
57	    - CodeBERT fine-tuned on Devign (off the shelf, cross-dataset, argmax, 512 tokens) (p. 6);
58	    - CodeBERT (125M) fine-tuned on PrimeVul's training split, with the threshold selected on the validation split (p. 10–11).
59	  - [V] **CodeQL was not run.** PrimeVul functions are isolated snippets with no build, so no CodeQL database can be built (p. 10–11).
60	
61	## 4. Dataset and sample
62	- Data source(s): [V] PrimeVul test split (C/C++): 24,788 functions after loading, 549 vulnerable — "a realistic 1:44 class ratio" (p. 4).
63	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] N = 1549 functions: all 549 vulnerable plus 1000 seeded-random safe functions (p. 4). [I] Prevalence in the evaluated sample is 35.4% (549/1549). This is **not** 50/50, although the text once calls it "balanced by construction" (p. 8). [V] The effective N per model is 1526–1549 because parse failures are excluded (p. 6).
64	- Sampling / selection method:
65	  - [V] Label-stratified sample fixed by seed (p. 4).
66	  - [V] Two further near-disjoint safe pools (<6% overlap) were drawn for robustness (p. 19).
67	  - [V] LLM inputs were truncated to 8000 characters. This affects 105/1549 functions and 87/549 (15.8%) of the vulnerable ones; non-LLM baselines see untruncated code (p. 4).
68	  - [V] All CVEs date from 2008–2022 and predate the models' training cutoffs (p. 24). [V] The PrimeVul training split contains no evaluated function or function body (up to whitespace) (p. 10, p. 25).
69	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Released on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.21391073): harness, configurations, sampled function IDs, price snapshot, energy sweep, baseline scores and aggregated results (p. 26). [V] PrimeVul is fetched from its original authors by script; the fine-tuned checkpoint is regenerable by script (p. 26).
70	
71	## 5. Experimental setup
72	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
73	  - [V] Harness and decoding: a test-driven harness with 82 automated tests; temperature 0, seed 12345, one generation per item; output budget 64 tokens in the matched configuration (256 for two frontier models in the first epoch) (p. 6, p. 29).
74	  - [V] Cost: computed from logged input/output tokens × list price at a pinned provider, with gateway fallbacks disabled (p. 5).
75	  - [V] Provider price dispersion: up to 14.4× for DeepSeek-V3.2 (USD 0.209–3.000 per million input tokens) (p. 5, Table 3).
76	  - [V] Energy (p. 5):
77	    - FLOP estimate E ≈ 2·N_active·T·ε for API-served models;
78	    - measured with the NVML energy counter on a dedicated NVIDIA H200 for locally servable open models (concurrency 1, idle-subtracted "active" energy);
79	    - plus a concurrency sweep c = 1/8/32/64 (p. 14, Table 9).
80	  - [V] Latency: client-side under concurrency 10, so it conflates queueing (p. 30).
81	  - [V] Statistics: stratified paired bootstrap of balanced-accuracy differences (20,000 resamples, seed 12,345) with Holm correction over a 9-comparison primary family and a 15-comparison strict family (p. 6, p. 28).
82	- Code availability: [V] The harness and configurations are released (p. 6, p. 26).
83	
84	## 6. Evaluation metrics
85	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
86	  - [V] **Balanced accuracy** is the primary metric, because accuracy is dominated by the always-safe classifier (0.646 accuracy, above every LLM) and both trivial classifiers score exactly 0.5 on it (p. 6).
87	  - [V] MCC and F1 are also reported (p. 6).
88	  - [V] Deployment metrics at 1:44 prevalence are derived from the prevalence-invariant TPR/FPR (p. 8, Table 5):
89	    - precision; false positives per true positive (FP/TP);
90	    - alerts and found vulnerabilities per 1000 functions;
91	    - **USD per true positive** and **kJ per true positive**.
92	  - [V] Elicited 0–100 confidence gives ROC-AUC where usable. VD-Score is declined because the coarse score grids cannot reach its 0.5% FPR point (p. 9–10).
93	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
94	  - [V] Paired bootstrap 95% CIs and Holm-adjusted p for open-vs-frontier gaps (p. 27, Table A1).
95	  - [V] Wilson-based 95% CIs on precision at deployment prevalence for the non-LLM baselines (p. 10, Table 7).
96	  - [V] Robustness: Spearman rank correlation across prompts and draws (p. 19, Table 13).
97	  - [V] Output-budget effects are tested with a paired bootstrap (p. 16, Table 10).
98	
99	## 7. Key findings
100	1. **Detection quality, first epoch** — [V] Balanced accuracy / F1 per model, direct mode, N = 1549 (p. 7, Table 4). [V] F1 range across LLMs is 0.405–0.615 vs always-vulnerable F1 0.523 (p. 7, Table 4).
101	
102	   | Model | Bal. acc. (95% CI) | F1 |
103	   |---|---|---|
104	   | DeepSeek-V3.2 | 0.676 (0.654–0.697) | 0.615 |
105	   | Gemma-3-4B | 0.653 | 0.590 |
106	   | GLM-5 | 0.637 | 0.596 |
107	   | Gemini-3.1-Pro | 0.623 | 0.591 |
108	   | GPT-5.1 | 0.617 | 0.560 |
109	   | Claude-Sonnet-5 | 0.616 | 0.582 |
110	   | Llama-3.3-70B | 0.604 | 0.578 |
111	   | Qwen3-Coder-30B | 0.511 | 0.405 |
112	
113	2. **Open vs frontier significance** — [V] DeepSeek-V3.2 significantly beats all three frontier models: +0.054 to +0.060 balanced accuracy, Holm p < 5×10⁻⁴ (p. 6, p. 27, Table A1).
114	   - [V] Gemma-3-4B beats Claude-Sonnet-5 (+0.037, Holm p = 0.032); the other top-open gaps are not significant (p. 7, p. 27).
115	   - [V] Qwen3-Coder-30B is indistinguishable from chance (MCC 0.022, CI −0.03 to 0.07) (p. 7).
116	3. **Budget-matched second epoch (Family A)** — [V] Balanced accuracy / MCC: DeepSeek-V3.2 0.711 / 0.403; GLM-5 0.669 / 0.352; Gemma-3-4B 0.653 / 0.297; Claude-Sonnet-5 0.653 / 0.321; GPT-5.1 0.615 / 0.225; Llama 0.609 / 0.267; Qwen 0.568 / 0.136; Gemini 0.606 / 0.252, on only the 54.2% of tasks it answered (p. 17, Table 11).
117	   - [V] Claude equals Gemma (+0.0003, p = 0.98) (p. 17).
118	   - [V] Absolute numbers shifted by up to 0.06 between epochs seven weeks apart ("service drift") (p. 7–8, p. 20).
119	4. **Reasoning mode** — [V] Reasoning helps every frontier model (Claude +0.032, GPT-5.1 +0.044, Gemini +0.096) but hurts DeepSeek-V3.2 (−0.133, p < 10⁻⁴) and does not help GLM-5 (−0.019, n.s.); it costs 4.5–12.1× more per task (p. 17–18, Table 12).
120	   - [V] Best observed: DeepSeek 0.711 (direct) vs Claude 0.685 and Gemini 0.680 (reasoning); DeepSeek vs Claude p = 0.081 (p. 17).
121	   - [V] Reasoning lowers DeepSeek's specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 (p. 20).
122	5. **Prompt sensitivity dominates** — [V] Two paraphrases move balanced accuracy by up to 0.088 and produce three different winners (DeepSeek 0.711, Claude 0.741, GLM-5 0.700); Spearman ρ vs anchor = 0.381 and 0.810 (p. 19–20, Table 13).
123	   - [V] Safe-pool redraws move scores ≤0.015 (ρ = 1.000) (p. 19).
124	   - [V] Temperature-0 verdict agreement is 88.3–100%; only Gemma is exactly reproducible (p. 19).
125	6. **SAST baselines on the same functions** (p. 7, p. 10, Table 4, Table 7) — balanced accuracy / recall / specificity / precision at 1:44:
126	   - [V] Flawfinder risk≥1: 0.589 / 0.271 / 0.907 / 6.20%; risk≥4: 0.523 / 0.055 / 0.992 / 13.40%.
127	   - [V] Cppcheck: 0.548–0.592 balanced accuracy; precision 2.46–3.77%.
128	   - [V] Semgrep severity≥INFO: 0.514 / 0.031 / 0.998 / 25.96% (CI 5.7–66.9%). It flags 19 of 1549 functions with 17 TP and 2 FP (p. 11).
129	   - [V] Flawfinder is "ahead of every LLM at every threshold" on deployment precision but finds almost nothing (p. 9, p. 23).
130	7. **Fine-tuned DL baseline beats every LLM** — [V] CodeBERT-PrimeVul (125M, validation-tuned threshold) reaches balanced accuracy 0.765, MCC 0.526, recall 0.709, specificity 0.821, precision 8.23% at 1:44 (CI 6.9–9.7) and ROC-AUC 0.845 (p. 10, Table 7; p. 10–11). [V] CodeBERT-Devign (cross-dataset) collapses to 0.518, flagging 97% of functions (p. 7, p. 23). [V] At argmax 0.5 the PrimeVul detector predicts all-safe because no score exceeds 0.372. The authors "nearly reported" this artefact as evidence that trained detectors are no better than LLMs (p. 11).
131	8. **Deployment at 1:44 prevalence** — [V] Every LLM's precision is 2.3–3.8% vs 2.21% for always-flag; FP/TP ranges from 25.6 (DeepSeek) to 41.9 (Qwen); models alert on 43–75% of functions (p. 8, Table 5). [A] "Neither is ready for independent use" (p. 9).
132	9. **Cost per task** — [V] USD/task, first epoch (p. 7, Table 4); SAST and CodeBERT-Devign cost ≈0:
133	
134	   | Model | USD/task |
135	   |---|---|
136	   | DeepSeek-V3.2 | 0.00017 |
137	   | Gemma-3-4B | 0.00004 |
138	   | GLM-5 | 0.00048 |
139	   | Gemini-3.1-Pro | 0.00448 |
140	   | GPT-5.1 | 0.00139 |
141	   | Claude-Sonnet-5 | 0.00441 |
142	   | Llama-3.3-70B | 0.00008 |
143	   | Qwen3-Coder-30B | 0.00006 |
144	
145	   - [V] Family A cost (p. 17, Table 11): DeepSeek 0.00015, Claude 0.00265, Gemini 0.00219 USD/task.
146	   - [V] Gemma matches Claude's Family A quality at 1/66 of the cost; DeepSeek beats Claude at 1/18 (p. 17).
147	10. **Energy per task** — [V] J/task (p. 7, Table 4); frontier values are FLOP estimates at an assumed 100B active parameters, with the 25–400B sweep in brackets:
148	
149	    | Model | J/task | Source |
150	    |---|---|---|
151	    | DeepSeek-V3.2 | 526 | estimated |
152	    | Gemma-3-4B | 64 | estimated |
153	    | GLM-5 | 424 | estimated |
154	    | Gemini-3.1-Pro | 1966 [492–7865] | estimated |
155	    | GPT-5.1 | 1332 [333–5329] | estimated |
156	    | Claude-Sonnet-5 | 2489 [622–9955] | estimated |
157	    | Llama-3.3-70B | 738 | measured |
158	    | Qwen3-Coder-30B | 88 | measured |
159	
160	    - [V] Concurrency sweep on an H200 (c = 1 → 64), J/task: Gemma 84.4 → 3.8; Qwen 84.0 → 7.5; Llama 739.9 → 74.2. The FLOP estimator overstates batched energy by 5.4–16.9× (p. 14, Table 9).
161	    - [A] API-served energies are "most likely" overstated by about an order of magnitude (p. 14).
162	11. **Cost and energy per detected vulnerability (G6)** — [V] At 1:44 prevalence (p. 8, Table 5):
163	
164	    | Model | USD per TP | kJ per TP |
165	    |---|---|---|
166	    | Gemma-3-4B | 0.003 | 3.7 |
167	    | Llama-3.3-70B | 0.004 | 44.8 |
168	    | Qwen3-Coder-30B | 0.006 | 4.0 |
169	    | DeepSeek-V3.2 | 0.009 | 28.4 |
170	    | GLM-5 | 0.023 | 20.3 |
171	    | GPT-5.1 | 0.082 | 78.3 |
172	    | Gemini-3.1-Pro | 0.210 | 92.4 |
173	    | Claude-Sonnet-5 | 0.212 | 119.6 |
174	
175	    - [V] Flawfinder: ≈0 cost per TP (p. 8, Table 5).
176	    - [V] USD/TP is not reported for CodeBERT-PrimeVul ("negligible inference cost", p. 11) or for Cppcheck/Semgrep (pp. 8–11).
177	    - [V] **Human triage effort is not included**: these are compute costs per TP surfaced, with 25.6–41.9 false positives per TP (p. 8).
178	12. **Self-hosting economics** — [V] At concurrency 64 on one H200, self-hosting is cheaper than the API for Gemma and Qwen (0.15–0.36× API price) (p. 22, Table 14). For Llama-3.3-70B it is 0.63× on owned hardware but 1.50× on a rented card. These are GPU-time-only assumptions (USD 3.50/h rented; USD 1.46/h owned).
179	13. **Contamination gradient** — [V] Recall on pre-2020 CVEs is 7–15 points higher than on 2021–2022 CVEs for better-balanced models (e.g. GPT-5.1 0.88 vs 0.73; DeepSeek 0.90 vs 0.81) (p. 24). [A] This is "consistent with some memorization" (p. 24).
180	14. **Elicited confidence** — [V] Only Claude used the requested probability scale (ROC-AUC 0.814); three models reported verdict confidence instead (converted AUC 0.69–0.76); DeepSeek emitted −1 on 1409/1549 tasks; Gemini produced a parseable pair on 1.2% of tasks (p. 9, Table 6).
181	15. **Trivial-baseline comparison** — [I] Our reading of Table 4 (p. 7):
182	    - Sample (35.4% positive): best LLM F1 0.615 is only +0.092 above always-vulnerable F1 0.523; Qwen (0.405) is below it. The 0.667 balanced-data reference does not apply at this prevalence.
183	    - At 1:44 prevalence, our calculation from Table 5 TPR and precision (p. 8): always-flag F1 ≈ 0.043; best LLM (DeepSeek) F1 ≈ 0.072; CodeBERT-PrimeVul ≈ 0.147; Flawfinder risk≥1 ≈ 0.101. Flawfinder's F1 is above every LLM's at deployment prevalence.
184	
185	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
186	- [A] Energy is measured for only some open models; frontier energy rests on an untested active-parameter assumption and is reported as a sensitivity range (p. 23).
187	- [A] Configuration asymmetries: Gemini cannot run without reasoning; two frontier models needed larger output budgets in the main run (p. 24).
188	- [A] Latency is confounded by queueing (p. 24).
189	- [A] Training-data contamination: all CVEs are 2008–2022 and may appear in pre-training; absolute scores "may be optimistic"; a post-cutoff restriction is planned (p. 24).
190	- [A] One prompt, one draw and one generation in the headline table; variation across datasets and task formulations remains unbounded (p. 24).
191	- [A] Serving-layer dependence (p. 24–25):
192	  - price spread up to 14×;
193	  - two silent serving faults: billed empty outputs, and a reasoning flag ignored with HTTP 200;
194	  - quality is robust to provider and precision for Llama (0.599–0.609).
195	- [A] CodeQL cannot be applied to unbuildable function snippets (p. 25).
196	- [A] Scope: one dataset, one task formulation, function level only; other languages and statement-level localisation are future work (p. 25).
197	- [A] "No result here should be read as evidence that function-level vulnerability triage is ready for independent use" (p. 26).
198	
199	## 9. Limitations we identified
200	- [I] **Internal inconsistencies from revision** (the paper went through at least one major review round, p. 1, pp. 16–19):
201	  - Gemma-3-4B is said to be incompatible with the local vLLM/CUDA build, so its energy is FLOP-estimated (p. 6, p. 15). Yet Table 9 reports a measured concurrency sweep for Gemma (p. 14), and the abstract says three open models were measured (p. 1), while p. 5 says two.
202	  - The limitations list says a fine-tuned PrimeVul detector "is the remaining gap" (p. 25), but Section 4.4 reports exactly such a detector (p. 10–11).
203	  - The reasoning cost multiplier is "2.5 to 7.6 times" on p. 24 vs 4.5–12.1× in Table 12 (p. 18); these are different epochs, but the text does not say so.
204	  - The sample is called "balanced by construction" (p. 8) although it is 35.4% positive (p. 4).
205	  - These are reporting slips, not evidence of wrong numbers, but readers should cite table values rather than prose.
206	- [I] **The SAST arm is weak by design for C/C++.** Flawfinder, Cppcheck and Semgrep community rules on isolated functions, with no CodeQL, Infer or commercial tools (p. 10–11). The comparison is LLM vs lightweight function-level SAST, not vs semantic whole-program SAST.
207	- [I] **Not post-cutoff** (CVEs 2008–2022, p. 24), and the measured recall gradient by CVE year suggests memorisation. The LLM-vs-fine-tuned comparison is also asymmetric: the fine-tuned model is in-distribution, while the LLMs are zero-shot (p. 11).
208	- [I] **Cost per TP excludes triage.** With 25.6–41.9 FP per TP (p. 8), analyst time would dominate compute cost (cents per TP). The paper's USD/TP therefore understates the practical cost per confirmed vulnerability by a large factor.
209	- [I] **Unnamed gateway** and preview model identifiers (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`, p. 29) limit long-term reproducibility. The service drift of up to 0.06 between epochs (p. 20) shows API results are time-stamped observations.
210	- [I] **Function-level, C/C++ only** — no repository context. The truncation at 8000 characters affects 15.8% of positives (p. 4).
211	- [I] **AI-assisted writing and code.** The authors used Claude Opus 5/Sonnet 5 to draft text and write Python code (p. 27), and Claude-Sonnet-5 is one of the evaluated models. This is disclosed and the data are stated to be the authors' own; we note it for transparency, not as a conflict.
212	
213	## 10. Threats to validity
214	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
215	  - [V] Train/test separation for CodeBERT-PrimeVul is verified: no evaluated function or body is in training (p. 25).
216	  - [V] Thresholds are tuned on validation, not test (sweeping on test would give 0.777 vs the reported 0.765) (p. 11).
217	  - [V] Contamination is not controlled but is measured as a recall gradient by CVE year (p. 24).
218	  - [V] Epoch drift is handled by within-epoch comparisons (p. 16–18).
219	  - [V] Parse failures are excluded, not recoded (p. 27).
220	- External (generalisability of sample/context):
221	  - [V] One dataset (PrimeVul), C/C++, function level (p. 25).
222	  - [I] It is unclear whether results hold for repository-level detection or other languages.
223	  - [I] Model versions are a 2026 snapshot.
224	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
225	  - [V] Balanced accuracy is chosen deliberately; the paper shows its ranking differs from the precision ranking at deployment prevalence (GPT-5.1 3rd on precision, 5th on balanced accuracy) (p. 8–9).
226	  - [I] PrimeVul labels are "near-human-accuracy" per its authors (p. 3), but no own label audit was done.
227	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance):

19	                                            Abstract
20	                                            Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to software vulnerability detection,
21	                                            but evaluations report accuracy while ignoring inference cost and energy and under-
22	                                            represent open-weight models relative to proprietary systems. We benchmark eight LLMs,
23	                                            three frontier, and five open-weight on a stratified 1549-function subset of label-clean
24	                                            PrimeVul, treating cost and energy as first-class axes alongside detection quality. Cost is
25	                                            measured directly; energy is measured on-GPU across a concurrency sweep for three locally
26	                                            servable open models and FLOP-estimated with a sensitivity range for the API-served ones.
27	                                            Efficiency is the robust finding: open-weight models occupy the quality-efficiency Pareto
28	                                            frontier in every configuration tested, and no frontier model is Pareto-optimal; this is a
29	                                            4-billion-parameter model matching the best frontier system’s quality at one sixty-sixth of
30	                                            the list price. On quality, at a matched output budget, the best open model significantly
31	                                            exceeds every frontier model (0.711 balanced accuracy against 0.606–0.653), although the
32	                                            strongest frontier system is level with the next two open models. Two findings bound the
33	                                            practical reading. A 125-million-parameter detector fine-tuned on PrimeVul outperforms
34	                                            all eight LLMs (0.765), so where in-distribution labels exist, a small task-specific model is
35	                                            the better instrument. It should be noted that nothing here is deployment-ready: at the
36	                                            natural 1:44 prevalence, precision is 2.3–8.2%.

72	                               Second, security evaluations lean heavily on proprietary frontier models. A recent
73	                          review of offensive-security LLM studies found that proprietary systems appeared in
74	                          nearly every publication, while open-weight models were used in roughly half [4]. Yet,
75	                          open-weight models are precisely what many security teams need. They allow on-premises
76	                          deployment for privacy, compliance, and data-residency reasons, without sending sensitive
77	                          source code to an external service [8].
78	                               This paper brings the two concerns together. We benchmark eight contemporary LLMs,
79	                          a spread of open-weight and frontier systems, on realistic vulnerability detection, reporting
80	                          cost and energy as first-class axes, with latency as a confounded secondary measure. We
81	                          also calibrate the LLM results against non-LLM reference points, a static analyzer, and a
82	                          learned detector to gauge absolute difficulty. Our contributions are as follows:
83	                          •    A cost- and energy-aware benchmark of open-weight versus frontier LLMs on the
84	                               label-clean PrimeVul dataset [1], with a reproducible, test-driven measurement harness
85	                               and non-LLM reference points (Section 3).
86	                          •    Empirical evidence that open-weight models occupy the quality and efficiency Pareto
87	                               frontier, from a 4-billion-parameter model at the efficiency end to a sparse mixture
88	                               of experts at the quality end, while no frontier model is Pareto-optimal. We separate
89	                               two claims of different strength. The efficiency advantage is configuration-invariant: it
90	                               holds in every configuration we tested and widens when the frontier models are al-
91	                               lowed their native reasoning mode (Section 4). The quality advantage is configuration-
92	                               specific: at a matched direct-answer budget, the best open model significantly beats
93	                               every frontier model, but granting the frontier its native reasoning mode raises the
94	                               strongest frontier system to statistical parity with it, at several times the cost. The de-
95	                               fensible summary is, therefore, a decisive efficiency advantage together with quality
96	                               competitiveness, not quality dominance.
97	                          •    A precise account of what can and cannot be measured for closed API models. We
98	                               measure cost and latency directly throughout, measure energy on-GPU for the two
99	                               locally servable open models, and provide a bounded, assumption-explicit FLOP
100	                               estimate of energy for the API-only models. The measured points are consistent with
101	                               that estimate to within roughly a factor of two (Sections 3 and 4.6).
102	                                We are explicit that these results are a first, deployment-realistic snapshot and that
103	                          quality in absolute terms is poor. At PrimeVul’s natural 1:44 prevalence, every model we
104	                          tested raises roughly twenty-six false alarms per true finding, so the comparison identifies
105	                          the least miscalibrated model rather than a usable one; Section 4.3 quantifies this before any
106	                          deployment reading is drawn from the rankings. Energy is measured directly for the two
107	                          locally servable open models and FLOP-estimated with a sensitivity range for the API-only
108	                          models. Section 5 details these limitations and the extensions they invite.

111	                          2.1. LLMs for Vulnerability Detection
112	                               Benchmarks for LLM-based vulnerability detection have proliferated. Meta’s CyberSe-
113	                          cEval suite evaluates insecure-code generation and broader cyber-safety [3]. SecVulEval
114	                          provides a large, de-duplicated, CVE-grounded C/C++ set with statement-level labels [2].
115	                          Independent evaluations temper early optimism. Ullah et al. found that leading LLMs
116	                          cannot yet reliably identify or reason vulnerabilities [9]. Steenhoek et al. reported only
117	                          54.5% balanced accuracy for state-of-the-art models on this task [10], a picture our results
118	                          corroborate. A recurring and central concern is label quality. The C/C++ datasets under-
119	                          pinning this literature have grown successively larger and cleaner, from Devign [11] and
120	                          Big-Vul [12] to the de-duplicated DiverseVul [13]. Even so, many widely used sets carry
121	                          substantial label noise and cross-split duplication, which inflates reported performance

137	                          2.2. Efficiency and Energy of LLM Inference
138	                               The energy and climate cost of large models has been a concern since at least the
139	                          training-time analysis of Strubell et al. [16], and measuring the cost of inference is now an
140	                          active area in its own right. Direct energy measurement on datacenter GPUs has been
141	                          reported for open models [17,18], and standardized power-measurement methodology
142	                          exists at the systems level [6]. A well-documented pitfall is that NVIDIA’s sampled power
143	                          interface substantially under-samples short kernels, which motivates counter-based mea-
144	                          surement [19]. For closed API models, energy cannot be measured directly. Infrastructure-
145	                          aware estimation frameworks instead bound it from public performance data and hardware
146	                          assumptions [20]. Efficiency has also entered general LLM benchmarks as a first-class
147	                          axis [5,7]. Our methodology reuses this rigor and applies it within a security-detection
148	                          benchmark, where, as Section 2.3 sets out, energy has not previously been reported as a
149	                          per-task evaluation axis.

152	                               Cost has recently begun to appear in LLM security evaluations. Lira et al. assessed the
153	                          effectiveness and inference cost of four proprietary models on interprocedural vulnerability
154	                          detection over ReposVul [21], and other recent work has compared open and frontier
155	                          models on security detection tasks, including web vulnerability detection in WordPress
156	                          plugins [22] and dual-mode function- and application-level detection [23]. This is the
157	                          immediate context for our study, and it is moving quickly.

196	                          3. Materials and Methods
197	                          3.1. Task and Dataset
198	                                We use binary function-level vulnerability detection. Given a C/C++ function,
199	                          the model answers whether it contains a vulnerability. We draw from the PrimeVul test
200	                          split [1] (24,788 functions after loading, of which 549 are vulnerable, a realistic 1:44 class
201	                          ratio). Because the test split contains only 549 vulnerable functions, a label-stratified sample
202	                          balances at most to 1098. We, therefore, evaluate on a stratified sample of N = 1549 (all
203	                          549 vulnerable functions plus 1000 safe functions), fixed by seed for reproducibility. For the
204	                          LLMs, function inputs are truncated to a fixed budget of 8000 characters to bound cost. This
205	                          affects 6.8% of the sample (105 of 1549 functions), and because vulnerable functions are
206	                          longer on average, 15.8% of them (87 of 549) are truncated. Where the vulnerable statement
207	                          falls beyond the budget, truncation caps achievable recall independently of model quality,
208	                          so the absolute recall figures are conservative. The two non-LLM baselines (Section 3.4)
209	                          instead see the untruncated function; so, on long inputs, they are, if anything, advantaged
210	                          relative to the LLMs. Each model is prompted to answer with a verdict first, followed by
211	                          an optional explanation. A lenient parser extracts the verdict, and outputs that yield no
212	                          parseable verdict are recorded as parse failures rather than silently counted as “safe”.
213	
214	                          3.2. Models
215	                               We evaluate eight models spanning parameter scale and provenance (Table 2). All are
216	                          served through a unified OpenAI-compatible API gateway. Frontier models are proprietary,
217	                          while open-weight models are publicly available and, in principle, self-hostable. Reasoning-
218	                          capable models are run in a direct-answer configuration where the provider permits it.
219	                          Gemini-3.1-Pro exposes no non-reasoning mode and is, therefore, run with reasoning
220	                          enabled; Claude-Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.1 are run with reasoning disabled.

236	                                We treat detection quality, cost, and energy as co-equal evaluation axes and also
237	                          report latency. Because the open-weight models here are also accessed through the API

280	                                Two methodological consequences follow, and both are new in this revision. First,
281	                          every run pins its provider explicitly with gateway fallbacks disabled, so the configured
282	                          per-token price is the price actually charged and the served numerics are fixed; the pinned
283	                          provider and quantization for each model are listed in Appendix B. This also guards against
284	                          a failure we observed directly: one provider for Qwen3-Coder-30B billed output tokens
285	                          while returning empty content, which would have been scored as a parse failure and
286	                          silently understated the model. Second, we report the cost axis as an operating point with
287	                          a provider attached rather than as an intrinsic model property, and we treat the provider
288	                          spread as its uncertainty. Energy, in contrast, is a physical quantity that does not depend
289	                          on who is selling it, which is the central reason we regard it as the sounder efficiency axis
290	                          of the two.

658	                          A Task-Specific Detector Beats Every LLM We Tested
659	                                The fine-tuned CodeBERT breaks that frontier, and this is the most consequential
660	                          result of our revision. With its decision threshold selected on PrimeVul’s validation split
661	                          and applied unchanged to the evaluated functions, it reaches 0.765 balanced accuracy,
662	                          MCC 0.526, and 8.2% precision at deployment prevalence while still recovering 71% of
663	                          the vulnerable functions. Every one of those figures is better than the best LLM in our
664	                          roster: DeepSeek-V3.2 scores 0.676, MCC 0.344, and 3.8% precision. It is not a marginal
665	                          difference. On MCC, the threshold-invariant metric, the 125-million-parameter encoder
666	                          exceeds the best of eight general-purpose models by more than 50%, and it does so at
667	                          negligible inference cost on a single commodity GPU.
668	                                Two methodological points keep this honest. First, the threshold matters enormously
669	                          and must not be tuned on the evaluation set: sweeping the threshold on the evaluated func-
670	                          tions themselves would have reported 0.777, and we report 0.765 because the 0.777 figure
671	                          describes the best a threshold could have achieved rather than what the detector achieves.
672	                          The gap is small here (0.013), which tells us the threshold transfers between splits, but it
673	                          is the kind of optimism that is easy to publish accidentally. Second, and more impor-
674	                          tantly, our first attempt at this baseline produced 0.500 balanced accuracy with recall of
675	                          exactly zero, and we nearly reported it as evidence that trained detectors fare no better
676	                          than LLMs on PrimeVul. That was an artifact: under unweighted cross-entropy on a split
677	                          that is 2.77% positive, predicting “safe” everywhere is the optimum, and no score in the
678	                          model’s output ever exceeded 0.372, so an argmax decision rule could not have produced a
679	                          positive prediction whatever the model had learned. The ranking underneath was strong
680	                          all along (ROC-AUC 0.845). We record this because the failure mode is silent, produces a
681	                          plausible-looking number, and would have supported precisely the wrong conclusion.
682	                                The comparison does come with a condition, and it is the one that matters for practice.
683	                          The detector is trained on PrimeVul’s own training split and is, therefore, in-distribution,
684	                          while the LLMs are evaluated zero-shot. That is not an unfair comparison—it is the choice
685	                          an organization actually faces—but the two options have different prerequisites. A fine-
686	                          tuned detector requires several thousand labeled vulnerable functions from the target
687	                          distribution; an LLM requires none. Where such labels exist, our results say plainly that
688	                          a small task-specific model is the better and far cheaper instrument, and that the LLM
689	                          comparison in Section 4.2 is a comparison among LLMs rather than a search for the best
690	                          available detector. Where they do not, the LLM results stand on their own terms.
691	                                None of this makes the task solved. At deployment prevalence, the trained detector
692	                          still raises eleven false alarms per true finding, and its 8.2% precision, while more than
693	                          double the best LLM’s, is not a number any triage workflow absorbs unaided.

1130	                                     4.7.4. A Provider Silently Disabled a Requested Capability
1131	                                          The DeepSeek reasoning arm reported here is a corrective run, and the reason is
1132	                                     worth recording. Our first attempt pinned DeepSeek to the same provider used for its
1133	                                     direct arm. That provider returned HTTP 200 for every request and produced a mean of
1134	                                     131 output tokens against 1771 in the earlier epoch, with no reasoning trace: it had accepted
1135	                                     reasoning:{enabled:true} and ignored it. The gateway’s own capability metadata lists
1136	                                     that provider as reasoning-capable, so neither an error code nor the advertised parameters
1137	                                     revealed the problem; the only signal was an output length an order of magnitude below
1138	                                     expectation. Probing one task across five providers provided 158 output tokens at the
1139	                                     original provider and 3032, 3390, 4219, and 7487 at the others, and we re-ran the arm at
1140	                                     the cheapest provider that honors the flag, matched in precision to the original. Section 5.3
1141	                                     treats this as what it is: provider pinning buys reproducible pricing and numerics, but it
1142	                                     does not guarantee that a requested capability is actually exercised, and a silent no-op is
1143	                                     detectable only by checking the output against an expectation.

1249	                          4.9. Reasoning Versus Direct Answering: Replication Across Epochs
1250	                               Section 4.7 reports the reasoning comparison within a single epoch, which is the
1251	                          version we rely on. We ran the same comparison seven weeks earlier, before the anchor
1252	                          re-run revealed service drift, and report it here because it replicates the qualitative pattern
1253	                          on independent data.
1254	                               In that earlier epoch, reasoning raised balanced accuracy for every frontier model—Claude-
1255	                          Sonnet-5 from 0.616 to 0.646 (p = 0.013), GPT-5.1 from 0.617 to 0.660 (p = 0.002),
1256	                          and Gemini-3.1-Pro from a budget-limited 0.623 to 0.677—and helped neither open model,
1257	                          significantly hurting DeepSeek-V3.2 (0.676 to 0.608, −0.067, p < 0.001) while leaving GLM-
1258	                          5 unchanged within noise (−0.017, p = 0.08). The in-epoch measurement reproduces all
1259	                          five signs and the two significance patterns, with a larger penalty for DeepSeek (−0.133)
1260	                          and a slightly smaller gain for Claude.
1261	                               The mechanism is visible in the confusion matrices and is the same in both epochs:
1262	                          reasoning lowers DeepSeek’s specificity from 0.52 to 0.37, so a model that was already well
1263	                          balanced begins to over-flag. Reasoning is not a free improvement. It helps systems whose
1264	                          direct-mode calibration is poor, and degrades one whose calibration is already good.
1265	                               That two independent measurement epochs, seven weeks and one provider-pinning
1266	                          change apart, agree on every sign is the strongest evidence we have that the reasoning
1267	                          result is a property of the models rather than of a particular measurement. The absolute
1268	                          numbers differ by up to 0.06 between epochs, which is exactly why Section 4.7 draws its
1269	                          conclusions from one epoch alone.

1312	                          What Self-Hosting Actually Costs
1313	                                Our cost figures are gateway list prices for every model, so they answer “what does it
1314	                          cost to buy this inference?” rather than “what does it cost to run it?” Those are different
1315	                          questions, and conflating them would overstate the practical case for open weights. Three
1316	                          things must be kept apart: open-weight availability, our API-served evaluation, and genuine
1317	                          self-hosted economics. The first two we measure; the third is a model, which we now
1318	                          state explicitly.
1319	                                Take Llama-3.3-70B at FP8, the configuration we measured on the H200 and the
1320	                          strongest single-GPU on-premises candidate in our roster. Self-hosted cost per task is the
1321	                          hourly cost of the GPU divided by sustained throughput. We bracket the hourly cost at USD
1322	                          3.50 for an on-demand rented H200 and about USD 1.46 for owned hardware, the latter
1323	                          from a USD 32,000 card amortized over four years at 70% utilization plus roughly 750 W of
1324	                          draw at a 1.5 on-premises PUE and USD 0.22/kWh, a representative European industrial
1325	                          tariff. Against the measured API list price of USD 0.0000815 per task, break-even falls as
1326	                          follows (Table 14).
1327	                                The answer turns out to depend on model size, and it is more favorable to self-hosting
1328	                          than our earlier assumed-throughput estimate suggested. The two small models sustain
1329	                          45–64 tasks per second on a single card and are three to seven times cheaper to self-host
1330	                          than to buy, on rented or owned hardware alike. Llama-3.3-70B sustains only 8.0, which
1331	                          straddles the break-even: at 5.0 tasks per second on owned hardware, it is 1.6 times cheaper
1332	                          to self-host, but on a rented card, it is 1.5 times dearer than the gateway. So, an organization
1333	                          with its own hardware should self-host any of these models; one renting by the hour should
1334	                          self-host the small ones and buy 70B from an API.
1335	                                This refines rather than overturns our headline. The open models’ price advantage
1336	                          in Table 4 is still partly a market fact—open weights are served by many competing
1337	                          providers at high batch efficiency (Section 3), and that competition is not a property of
1338	                          the models—but the measured throughput shows the advantage is not only that. At the

1424	                          5.2. Why the Benchmark Is Hard
1425	                               No LLM exceeded 0.68 balanced accuracy, and none beat the trivial always-safe
1426	                          classifier on raw accuracy, an important sanity check on this imbalanced set. Two non-LLM
1427	                          reference points frame the difficulty (Table 4). A classical lexical static analyzer, Flawfinder,
1428	                          reaches 0.589 balanced accuracy, below every LLM except the near-chance Qwen3-Coder-
1429	                          30B. Because it flags conservatively (specificity 0.91), it is the only method here that beats
1430	                          the always-safe baseline on raw accuracy (0.682 against 0.646) at essentially zero cost.
1431	                          A learned detector, CodeBERT fine-tuned on the Devign dataset and applied off the shelf,
1432	                          does worse. It collapses to 0.518 balanced accuracy, flagging 97% of functions as vulnerable,
1433	                          which is essentially the always-vulnerable baseline. That collapse is itself informative
1434	                          rather than a weak comparison: it is precisely PrimeVul’s thesis that a model trained on an
1435	                          older, noisier dataset does not transfer to its clean, de-duplicated test set [1,14,15], and we
1436	                          therefore report it as a cross-dataset transfer reference point rather than as a competitive
1437	                          detector. Section 4.4 adds baselines that are not handicapped in this way.
1438	                               On balanced accuracy, the best LLMs (DeepSeek-V3.2, 0.676) outperform both of
1439	                          these reference points—among the methods evaluated here. The ordering reverses on
1440	                          precision at deployment prevalence, where Flawfinder is ahead of every LLM at every
1441	                          threshold, reaching 13.4% against 2.3–3.8% at risk level 4 (Section 4.3). Which family
1442	                          looks better therefore depends entirely on the operating regime, and neither is adequate in
1443	                          either. All methods remain far from reliable, which is exactly what makes the benchmark
1444	                          meaningful. Several models default to flagging. Gemini-3.1-Pro and Claude-Sonnet-5
1445	                          among the frontier systems, and GLM-5 and Llama-3.3-70B among the open ones, all have
1446	                          specificity below 0.36, which in a triage setting translates into alert fatigue rather than
1447	                          useful signal. DeepSeek-V3.2 and Gemma-3-4B lead the balanced metric because they
1448	                          pair competitive recall with specificity above 0.5. Qwen3-Coder-30B is also conservative
1449	                          (specificity 0.57) but couples it with a recall of only 0.45, so its balanced accuracy is barely
1450	                          above chance, and it gains nothing.

1576	                          6. Conclusions
1577	                               We benchmarked eight open-weight and frontier LLMs on label-clean vulnerability
1578	                          detection, measuring cost, latency, and energy alongside detection quality. Two findings of
1579	                          unequal strength follow, and separating them is the point.
1580	                               Efficiency is the firm one. Open-weight models occupy the quality and efficiency
1581	                          Pareto frontier; no frontier model is Pareto-optimal, and this holds in every configuration
1582	                          we tested, at roughly one-hundredth the list price and one to two orders of magnitude less
1583	                          energy per task. It survives the output budget, the prompt template, the safe-function draw,
1584	                          and the choice of reasoning mode, and it widens when the frontier models are allowed to

1609	                          labels exist, the evidence here says to fine-tune a small model rather than prompt a large
1610	                          one. Where they do not, the LLM ordering above stands on its own terms.

1612	                          natural 1:44 prevalence, precision reaches 2.3–3.8% for the LLMs and 8.2% for the trained

1615	                          analyzer is more precise than any LLM at every threshold, and finds almost nothing. These

1621	                          sured batched energy—and doing so per architecture, since dense and sparse models

1725	                                Balanced-accuracy differences are tested with a stratified paired bootstrap over
1726	                          20,000 resamples at seed 12,345. The 549 positive and 1000 negative task outcomes are
1727	                          resampled independently, preserving the design, and the same resampled indices are
1728	                          applied to both models so the comparison remains paired. Confidence intervals are
1729	                          percentile intervals over the resampled difference distribution; the two-sided p-value
1730	                          is 2 min{Pr(∆ ≤ 0), Pr(∆ ≥ 0)} under the bootstrap distribution. The bootstrap’s resolu-
1731	                          tion is therefore 1/20,000 = 5 × 10−5 : where no resample crosses zero we report a bound
1732	                          rather than a point estimate, because the procedure cannot distinguish 10−5 from 10−9 .
1733	                                Because this resampling draws the 1000 negatives with replacement, it also estimates
1734	                          the variability that would arise from having drawn a different safe sample of the same size,
1735	                          which is the quantity Section 5.3 refers to as draw-to-draw variance; Section 4.8 tests that
1736	                          estimate against genuinely independent draws.

1848	                                         Transient provider failures are retried with exponential backoff and full jitter, up to

1853	                                   serving-layer fault that, unretried, would have been scored as a model parse failure. Af-

1855	                                   fabricates a verdict. Every result row records the number of attempts spent, so retry-inflated

gap-report.md:168:  - *Open or Frontier?* (Computers 2026, doi:10.3390/computers15090623): eight LLMs vs a fine-tuned 125M detector on label-clean PrimeVul, reporting precision at 1:44 prevalence. **No SAST; not post-cutoff by design.**
gap-report.md:169:  - *A Real CVE-Backed Benchmark for WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Detection* (BDCC 2026, doi:10.3390/bdcc10090303): a static taint analyser plus ML/DL under plugin-grouped, de-duplicated CV. **No LLM.**
gap-report.md:190:  - **Baselines:** flag-all, random, and a function-length classifier (the WordPress study found it competitive).
gap-report.md:286:  - PHP: *WordPress plugin benchmark* (doi:10.3390/bdcc10090303): a static taint analyser vs ML/DL, no LLM. The taint analyser misses about 98% of vulnerabilities (abstract only).
gap-report.md:294:  - **Data:** about 60 real PHP CVEs (e.g. from the released WordPress-plugin benchmark data) or Go CVEs from the Go vulnerability database (OSV).
gap-report.md:298:  - **Threats:** label quality (the WordPress paper finds 48.8% of cleaned positives genuine, abstract only); small samples; tool coverage differences.
gap-report.md:310:  - *Open or Frontier?* (Computers 2026, doi:10.3390/computers15090623): measures cost and energy for 8 LLMs vs a fine-tuned detector, with precision at 1:44 prevalence. **No SAST, no triage effort.** This narrows the gap considerably.
gap-report.md:315:- Confidence: **low–medium**. The gap is narrowed by *Open or Frontier?*. What remains is the SAST arm and the triage-effort term.
gap-report.md:340:2. **doi:10.3390/bdcc10090303**, *WordPress plugin benchmark* (BDCC 2026). Leakage-controlled static vs learning-based detectors on PHP. Its conclusion that label quality outweighs family differences directly supports our RQ2 thesis, and it adds a non-C/Java language.

gap-report.md:287:  - *Vulnerability Detection with Interprocedural Context in Multiple Languages* (arXiv 2604.08417): LLMs only, C/C++/Python.
gap-report.md:311:  - *Vulnerability Detection with Interprocedural Context in Multiple Languages* (arXiv 2604.08417): cost per LLM configuration only.
    - du2026reducing: more languages [@du2026reducing, p. 10] [A];
    - xiong2026sifting: more languages and SAST tools [@xiong2026sifting, p. 20] [A];
    - li2026llm: broader languages and CWE classes [@li2026llm, p. 18] [A].
  - **The few multi-language studies are thin or lack SAST.**
    - The only multi-language LLM study (REEF, 7 languages) has no SAST arm [@shu2026evaluating, p. 7] [V].
    - zhou2024comparison covers Python with roughly 8–10 test CVEs per language [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6] [I].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q17, Q18, Q26 on OpenAlex/arXiv from 2024/2025; W8). Closest hits:
  - *RealVuln* (arXiv 2604.13764): Python, but intentionally vulnerable repositories and a vendor author.
  - JavaScript:
    - *LLMs Cannot Reliably Detect Vulnerabilities in JavaScript* (arXiv 2512.01255): LLM-focused benchmark;
    - *Exploring Automated Vulnerability Identification in JavaScript Code Using LLMs* (arXiv 2609.13816): snippet-level, LLM vs SAST.
  - PHP: *WordPress plugin benchmark* (doi:10.3390/bdcc10090303): a static taint analyser vs ML/DL, no LLM. The taint analyser misses about 98% of vulnerabilities (abstract only).
  - *Vulnerability Detection with Interprocedural Context in Multiple Languages* (arXiv 2604.08417): LLMs only, C/C++/Python.
  - *A Preliminary Study of LLMs for Multilingual Vulnerability Detection* (ISSTA companion 2025, doi:10.1145/3713081.3731746): PLMs vs LLMs, no SAST.

  We found no study comparing LLMs with SAST on real CVEs at repository level for PHP or Go, and only snippet-level or synthetic-repository evidence for JavaScript and Python (searches on 2026-11-12).
- Confidence: **low–medium**. Python and JavaScript are being filled quickly. The gap is clearest for PHP and Go.
- Potential contribution: tests whether the "LLM higher recall, lower precision" pattern holds in web languages, where injection CWEs (which LLMs handle best [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18]) dominate.
- Suggested study:
  - **Data:** about 60 real PHP CVEs (e.g. from the released WordPress-plugin benchmark data) or Go CVEs from the Go vulnerability database (OSV).
  - **Arms:** Semgrep (supports both languages), a language-specific SAST tool, and 2 open LLMs at file level with retrieved callers. Check CodeQL's supported-language list for the chosen language before planning a CodeQL arm.
  - **Metrics:** recall on known CVEs; precision on a manually labelled warning sample; cost.
  - **Analysis:** per-CWE recall with CIs.
  - **Threats:** label quality (the WordPress paper finds 48.8% of cleaned positives genuine, abstract only); small samples; tool coverage differences.
- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. The tools are free and build-free for PHP and Go. The main cost is manual labelling of warnings.

gap-report.md:107:## G1: Published results are not re-scored against trivial baselines or realistic prevalence; no shared evaluation protocol exists for comparing LLMs, SAST and DL
gap-report.md:150:## G2: No same-benchmark, leakage-controlled comparison of LLMs vs SAST vs fine-tuned DL on real, post-cutoff code
gap-report.md:201:## G3: True-positive loss in LLM filtering of SAST alarms is not controlled per CWE on real security alerts
gap-report.md:235:## G4: Hybrid LLM+SAST detectors lack independent replication that separates target, metric and labeller effects
gap-report.md:265:## G5: Repository-level, real-CVE LLM-vs-SAST evidence is missing for PHP, Go and JavaScript (Python only partly covered)
gap-report.md:301:## G6: No cost-per-confirmed-vulnerability comparison across LLM, SAST and DL including human triage effort
195:- **C1 Fine-tuned vs GPT-4.** Fine-tuned AIBugHunter (F1 94%) and CodeBERT (87%) far exceed prompted gpt-4 (29%) on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4], but GPT-4 CoT beats every fine-tuned model on pair-wise correctness on 564 PrimeVul pairs (12.94% vs ≤3.01%) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]. Differs in metric (F1 vs P-C), data (noisy random-split Big-Vul 1:20 vs de-duplicated time-split pairs) and model versions; Ding's own BigVul rows (F1 62.88–68.26%) agree with Fu [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. [I] Fine-tuned models exploit dataset artefacts rewarded by random splits [@risse2025top, p. 11]; on pairs all are below the 22.70% random reference, so the reversal reflects the benchmark more than the model family.
197:- **C3 LLM vs SAST.** LLMs win on 10 small C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10] and CASTLE C micro-programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]; at repository level LLMs detect more but flag up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7] (preprint), and general agents lead recall while specialised LLM detectors and SAST show near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75–100% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Differs in language, unit, synthetic vs real code, and scoring leniency (location rule only for LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]; CASTLE prompt reveals scoring [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]). [I] Synthetic suites match SAST rules, small programs fit LLM context, real repositories defeat both: no single winner.
198:- **C4 Does reasoning reduce false positives?** For: reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14]; RepoAudit precision 82.35–88.46% with reasoning backbones [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 16]. Against: DeepSeek R1 166 FP vs GPT-4o 116 in CASTLE's own table [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; thinking raises F1 via recall with unchanged accuracy and turns negative under DA/MA [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 8]; reasoning LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 37]. [I] Holds for OpenAI o-series in some settings only.
199:- **C5 Class balance flips rankings.** Balanced REEF: fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17]; imbalanced test: PLMs win (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 vs GPT-4o 0.4010) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @shu2026evaluating, p. 41]. yildiz F1 drops from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7]. [I] Balanced sets reward liberal flagging; balanced rankings do not transfer to deployment.
